title: 2 Cleaning SFO Weather Data
text:
Read in the weather data in this file with the correct relative file path after you move it to the instructed location.
There is a variable that has values that don’t make sense in the data context. Figure out which variable this is and clean it up by making those values missing using na_if().
Create a variable called dateInYear that indicates the day of the year (1-365) for each case. (Jan 1 should be 1, and Dec 31 should be 365).
Create a variable called month_name that shows the 3-letter abbreviation for each case.
Save the wrangled data to the data/processed/ folder using write_csv(). Name this file weather_clean.csv. Look up the documentation for this function by typing ?write_csv in the Console. You’ll need to write an appropriate relative path.

title: 3 Adv Data Viz
text:
Introduction 1

In this lesson, we are going to recreate NYTimes 2015 Temperature Visualization (html) using data from San Francisco (SFO) in 2011.


Screenshot of NYTimes 2015 Temperature Visualization

title: 3 Adv Data Viz
text:
Reading Data
Run the code chunk below to load the tidyverse package and read in the San Francisco weather data.

Codelibrary(tidyverse)
weather <- read_csv("https://mac-stat.github.io/data/sfo_weather.csv")

title: 3 Adv Data Viz
text:
Understanding Data
Below is the codebook of the data. Familiarize yourself with the meaning of each variable. Use the codebook as a reference when using the data.


Month: Month of the year (1-12)

Day: Day within the month (1-31)

Low/High: Low/high temperature this day

NormalLow/NormalHigh: Typical low/high temperature for this day of the year

RecordLow/RecordHigh: Record low/high temperature for this day of the year

LowYr/HighYr: Year in which the record low/high was observed

Precip: Amount of precipitation (inches) this day

RecordPrecip: Record amount of precipitation for this day of the year

PrecipYr: Year in which the record precipitation was observed

date: The actual date in 2011 for this day in YYYY-MM-DD format

dateInYear: What day of the year is it? (1-365)

Record: Logical (TRUE/FALSE) indicating whether this day had a high temperature record

RecordText: Text that displays the record high for this day ("Record high: ##")

RecordP: Logical (TRUE/FALSE) indicating whether this day had a precipitation record

CulmPrec: Cumulative precipitation for the month up to this day

title: 3 Adv Data Viz
text:
Exercise 1
Examine the NYTimes 2015 Temperature Visualization (html) then answer the following questions.
Data Storytelling


Relate the intro paragraph: “Scientists declared that 2015 was Earth’s hottest year on record…” to the design of the visualization. In particular, based on the intro paragraph,

What key message/claim does NYTimes want readers to be able to explore?

A culmination of temperature and weather data from 1981 to 2010, which is used to overlay against the temperature of 2015 data, showing a trend of increasingly warmer temperatures and extremer weather data.

How did this goal inform what information is displayed in the visualization?

NYtimes is trying to demonstrate or use data visualization supporting the claim that they’re making that “2015-2016” is one of the hottest year recorded at the TIME. Furthermore, graphs are showing only certain statistics which is useful in proving that claim.


Aesthetic Mapping


What specific variables (from the data codebook) underlie the visualization?

Temperature (F/C) on the Y Axis
Months on the Y Axis
Geom_bar pitted against negative + positive values

divided data through/ grouped data through shades/colors


Geom_line for the precipitation
Geom_polygon for the world map
I think the codebook is represented well in the NYtimes graphs, like all of it



How do these variables map to aesthetics of the visual elements, eg, position, size, shape, and color of glyphs?

Normal highs lows, Record highs lows, are represented through shade/fill, alpha?
Position not relative
Dotted lines to divide the months
Labels are clear
Legends
Search Bar for dataset selecting
Button switching between Celsius and Fahrenheit

title: 3 Adv Data Viz
text:
Exercise 2
Navigate the Geoms section of the ggplot2 reference page to find a geom that corresponds to the visual elements in the temperature plot. Using both the small thumbnail visuals on the right and the names of the geom’s, brainstorm some possibilities for geom’s you might use to recreate the temperature visualization.

geom_linerange

using layering or dodging (position)


geom_line for precipitation







NoteNavigating Documentation / Reference Pages



You need to navigate the geoms further by opening up their reference pages to understand if a particular geom is suitable for our task. Let’s look at the geom_point documentation page to learn how to read a documentation page.
The Usage section shows all of the possible inputs (arguments) to the geom. These are all of the ways that a geom can be customized. Just looking at the argument names can help give a hint as to what arguments might fit our needs.

mapping
data
stat
position

The Arguments section, on the other hand, explains in detail what each argument does and the possible values the argument can take. The mapping, data, and ... arguments will be the most commonly used by far.


mapping is the argument that is being used when we specify which variables should link or map to the plot aesthetics (the code inside aes()).

data is the argument where we specify the dataset containing the variables that the geom is using.

... is used for fixed aesthetics (ones that don’t correspond to a variable), eg, to set the color of all points, we use color = "red" and to set the size of all points, we use size = 3.

The Aesthetics section of a geom documentation page gives information on how the visual elements of the geom correspond to data. For example, the geom_point documentation page shows that x and y aesthetics are available. It also shows some new aesthetics like stroke.








Notedata Argument



Previously you have used one dataset per plot by specifying that as the first argument of ggplot(). However, multiple data sets can be passed into ggplot as shown in the example below.

Codedata(diamonds)

diamonds_avg_price <- diamonds |>
  group_by(carat) |>
  summarize(avg_price = mean(price)) |>
  arrange(carat)
diamonds_avg_price <- diamonds_avg_price[seq(1, nrow(diamonds_avg_price), 3), ]

ggplot(diamonds, aes(x = carat, y = price)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_point(
    data = diamonds_avg_price,
    aes(x = carat, y = avg_price),
    color = "deepskyblue",
    size = 3
  )









Look at the geom_linerange documentation page and start off your temperature visualization with the record lows and highs. Your plot should look like the one below. The hex code of the used light tan color is #ECEBE3.


SFO Weather Records in 2011


Codeggplot(weather) +
  geom_linerange(aes(x = dateInYear, ymin = RecordLow, ymax = RecordHigh), color = '#ECEBE3') +
  theme_classic()













TipKeyboard Shortcuts



As you work on this plot, try to use some new keyboard shortcuts. Focus on the following:

Insert code chunk: Ctrl+Alt+I (Windows). Option+Command+I (Mac).
Run current code chunk: Ctrl+Shift+Enter (Windows). Command+Shift+Return (Mac).
Run current line/currently selected lines: Ctrl+Enter (Windows). Command+Return (Mac).

Exercise 3
In your visualization, also display the usual temperatures (NormalLow and NormalHigh) and actual 2011 temperatures (Low and High). Your plot should look like the one below. The hex code of the color used for the usual temperatures is "#C8B8BA" and for the color used for actual temperatures is "#A90248".

Codeggplot(weather) + 
  geom_linerange(aes(x = dateInYear, ymin = RecordLow, ymax = RecordHigh), color = '#ECEBE3') +
  geom_linerange(aes(x = dateInYear, ymin = NormalLow, ymax = NormalHigh), color = '#C8B8BA') +
  geom_linerange(aes(x = dateInYear, ymin = Low, ymax = High), color = '#A90248') +
  theme_classic()

Finer control

  geom_rect(aes(xmin = dateInYear + 0.5, xmax = dateInYear - 0.5, ymin = RecordLow, ymax = RecordHigh), fill = '#ECEBE3') +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = dateInYear + 0.5, xmax = dateInYear - 0.5, ymin = NormalLow, ymax = NormalHigh), fill = '#C8B8BA') +
  geom_rect(aes(xmin = dateInYear + 0.5, xmax = dateInYear - 0.5, ymin = Low, ymax = High), fill = '#A90248') +
  theme_classic()

title: 3 Adv Data Viz
text:
Exercise 4
Recreate the visual demarcations of the months by adding vertical lines separating the months. Brainstorm how we might draw those vertical lines. What geom might we use? What subset of the data might we use in that geom layer to draw lines only at the month divisions?

Codeggplot(weather) + 
  geom_linerange(aes(x = date, ymin = RecordLow, ymax = RecordHigh), color = '#ECEBE3') +
  geom_linerange(aes(x = date, ymin = NormalLow, ymax = NormalHigh), color = '#C8B8BA') +
  geom_linerange(aes(x = date, ymin = Low, ymax = High), color = '#A90248') + 
  geom_vline(
    data = subset(weather, Day == 1), # this took a while to figure out
    aes(xintercept = date), 
    linetype = "dotted", 
    color = "grey")

title: 3 Adv Data Viz
text:
Exercise 5
Change the x-axis labels so that the month names display in the center of each month’s slice of the plot.






TipMonth Names



R has built-in variables called month.abb and month.name that contain abbreviated and full month names.



Codeggplot(weather) + 
  geom_linerange(aes(x = date, ymin = RecordLow, ymax = RecordHigh), color = '#ECEBE3') +
  geom_linerange(aes(x = date, ymin = NormalLow, ymax = NormalHigh), color = '#C8B8BA') +
  geom_linerange(aes(x = date, ymin = Low, ymax = High), color = '#A90248') + 
  geom_vline(
    data = subset(weather, Day == 1), # this took a while to figure out, so this will start a line every start of the month
    aes(xintercept = date), 
    linetype = "dotted", 
    color = "grey") + 
  scale_x_date(
    breaks = subset(weather, Day == 15)$date, # give or take its in the middle
    labels = month.abb)






Code# found hte scale_x_date function within https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/data-visualization.pdf

title: 3 Adv Data Viz
text:
Exercise 6
Create a precipitation plot that looks like the following. Note that

The triangles point to precipitation records–refer to the data codebook above for the RecordP variable.
The numbers on the plot indicate the total precipitation for the month–search the hjust and vjust options to adjust the alignment of the numbers.
The blue and tan colors hex codes are "#32a3d8" and "#ebeae2", respectively.



SFO Precipitation in 2011


Codemonth_labels <- weather %>%
  group_by(Month) %>%
  filter(dateInYear == max(dateInYear))

ggplot(weather, aes(x = dateInYear, y = CulmPrec)) +
  
  # 1. Add the tan filled area, grouped by month to create the gaps
  geom_area(aes(group = Month), fill = "#ebeae2") +
  
  # 2. Add the blue line on top of the area
  geom_line(aes(group = Month), color = "#32a3d8") +
  
  # 3. Add the downward-pointing triangles for records
  # We filter the data inline to only plot points where RecordP is TRUE
  geom_point(data = filter(weather, RecordP == TRUE), 
             shape = 25,        # Shape 25 is a downward-pointing triangle
             fill = "black", 
             size = 2) +
  
  # 4. Add the total precipitation numbers
  # Using the subset we created earlier so we don't plot text on every single day
  geom_text(data = month_labels, 
            aes(label = CulmPrec),
            vjust = -0.5,          # Moves text slightly above the line
            hjust = 0.5,           # Centers the text horizontally
            size = 3.5) +
  
  # 5. Apply a clean theme to remove gridlines and match the image
  theme_classic() +
  labs(x = "dateInYear", y = "CulmPrec")







Breaking Down Prompt and Output from Gemini - Prompt : “Can you guide me and complete the code in R, to recreate this plot with these instructions: - The triangles point to precipitation records–refer to the data codebook above for the RecordP variable. - The numbers on the plot indicate the total precipitation for the month–search the hjust and vjust options to adjust the alignment of the numbers. - The blue and tan colors hex codes are "#32a3d8" and "#ebeae2", respectively. using ggplot2 library” - Output : geom_area is new for me, but I understsand as it creates a density plot looking graph where it fills in the space in between the line and the x axis with the fill parameter. Furthermore, geom_text is new for me, but it seems intuitive enough as in being able to adjust the position of it. Gemini also data wrangled the data before hand, so that only the lastest of every every month row is available in a subset dataframe. Overall understandable, but if I was to do this myself would take some time working through documentations and trial/error with the parameters.

Initial view of the "joined" dataset signals my interest in the variables : price_gbp, hourly_wage, and city. While I want to explore spatial graphs, I find it problematic that there are no coordinates (long, lat) for me to use.

The first graph was to see whether the increase in wages is proportional to the increase in the price of a cappuccino. Although it's a moderately positive relationship (r ~ 0.477), which indicates that on average, the price of cappuccinos increases with the hourly wage per country. 

Then I ran a linear model to explore further. With only these two variables, we can see that, for each country, the average price of a single cappuccino doesn't depend on how much people earn per hour in that country (r^2 = 0.2269). Therefore,, there must be other drivers in this dataset that explain why the average value of a single cup of cappuccino is increasing or decreasing.

title: HW00 P2
text:
Second Viz
There's a column that distinguishes among urban, suburban, and rural. Therefore, using these characteristics as drivers of price, I want to see which region experiences the largest increase in cappuccino prices.

Codeindex_pivot <- cappuccino_index %>%
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(urban, suburban, rural), 
    names_to = "area",
    values_to = "is_present") %>%
  filter (is_present == TRUE) %>%
  select(-is_present)

# pivot longer so that I can get one singular column to work with for facet wrapping

index_pivot %>%
  ggplot (aes(x = area, y = price_gbp, fill = area)) + 
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5) + 
  theme_minimal() + 
  scale_fill_viridis_d() + # color blind options
  labs(title = "Cappuccino Prices by Area Type",
       subtitle = "Does the area in which you're in determine how much your coffee costs?",
       x = "Area Type",
       y = "Price",
       caption = "Data Source: TidyTuesday")







From afar, the boxplots seem to indicate little difference between the prices. However, if we scrutinize this, rural areas show the lowest and tightest distributions: lower prices on average, as well as less price variability from the minimum to the maximum a cup of coffee can go for. So there's more stable pricing. 

Suburban areas show more variability without reaching the highs of urban areas, with a steeper low than rural areas, indicating there's more competition among coffee prices. 

What's noticeable about the urban areas is their extreme outliers. This can indicate tourist areas, trends, and even really cheap places. Attributions to higher disposable income can also be explored!

These countries include: Djibouti, Egypt, India, Nicaragua, Oman, Pakistan, the Philippines, Qatar, Sri Lanka, and Vietnam. title: HW00 P2
text:
Forth Viz

Codemean_price <- mean(cappuccino_index$price, na.rm = TRUE)

cappuccino_index %>%
  mutate(reliability = ifelse(n < 10, "Small Sample (<10)", "Adequate Sample")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = n, y = price, color = reliability)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5, size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = mean_price, linetype = "dashed", color = "hotpink") +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Extreme price estimates are driven by small sample sizes",
    subtitle = "Dashed line shows the global average.",
    x = "Number of Cafés Sampled per City (n)",
    y = "Average Cappuccino Price (GBP)",
    caption = "Data Source: TidyTuesday")







Most of the extreme outliers are attributable to the small sample sizes. Therefore, we can simply say that, because some cities have fewer than 10 samples, the correlation is unreliable. It is not fair to say that hourly wage is a good/bad predictor of the price of a cup of cappuccino simply because some cities have more cafes sampled than others.

title: HW00 P2
text:
Confirmation of variations

Codevariability_model <- lm(price ~ n, data = cappuccino_index)
bptest(variability_model)


    studentized Breusch-Pagan test

data:  variability_model
BP = 11.772, df = 1, p-value = 0.0006014


If I were to use a simple linear model and summary, it would test the mean instead of the variance. We want to know whether small-sample-size cities are more likely to have extreme prices. Therefore, I did some googling and found out about bptest. The output p-value = 0.0006014 indicates that the variance is not constant in our dataset, and the spread of cappuccino prices is dependent on how many cafes were sampled.

title: HW00 P2
text:
Conclusion
To answer the research question: How does local hourly wage relate to cappuccino prices? We understand that the price of a cappuccino increases with the local hourly wage (in GBP); however, if that were the case, we would expect the hourly wage across different areas to differ as well. Viz Two, however, shows that there's no significant difference in cappuccino prices between the three areas. Furthermore, in Viz Three, most people spend about the same amount of time to afford a cup of cappuccino (10-15 minutes), with a few extreme outliers. This is consistent with the trends from Viz One, where if the time to afford a cup of cappuccino is relatively constant, then the hourly wage must also increase proportionally. We also understand that wage is not the only driving factor, and that much less than intuition would suggest, coupled with the reasons for those extreme outliers being a small sample size from different cities.
